blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a concerning side-channel attack where smartphones can be used to reconstruct objects being fabricated on factory floors, including CNC mills and 3D printers. The attack leverages phone sensors (audio and magnetometer) to capture machine sounds and movements, enabling the reconstruction of high-value intellectual property (IP) such as product designs. The paper demonstrates that even a simple phone call to an employee near the machine can facilitate the attack. The authors use signal processing and machine learning to analyze audio signatures, comparing them against a pre-recorded reference library of machine sounds at different angles. Domain constraints (e.g., layer-by-layer printing in 3D printers) and human assistance help refine the reconstruction. The study shows that even complex shapes (e.g., airplanes, stars, guns) can be reconstructed with reasonable accuracy, underscoring the vulnerability of manufacturing processes to espionage.
paper_title: Leave your phone at the door: side channels that reveal factory floor secrets
paper_abstract: Keystroke privacy is critical on mobile devices, as typed content often includes passwords and sensitive personal data. This paper revisits cross-app keystroke inference and shows that software sandboxing cannot prevent keystroke leakage at the physical layer because co-resident apps inevitably share the same hardware. Our insight is twofold. (1) Keystroke-induced vibrations propagate through the touchscreen and internal components and are captured by zeropermission motion sensors, preserving spatial traits tied to key positions. (2) Typing habits enable cross-app generalization, as users typically rely on the same virtual keyboard layout across apps, causing identical letters to yield similar vibration patterns. Based on these properties, we propose CaMi, a practical cross-app keystroke inference attack. CaMi learns letter-level vibration signatures using labeled samples in any commonly used app and then covertly collects motion sensor data to infer keystrokes typed in a target app. We implement CaMi on smartphones and tablets, and extensive experiments show high inference accuracy across devices. We also discuss potential software-level defenses.

When victim enters sensitive information in the foreground App with a virtual keyboard, the rogue App running in the background can collect the KiVi signals from accelerometer sensor and infer the victim’s input content with by querying a pre-trained KiVi-letter dictionary.
